Documentation

The documents every neon1 project keeps and how they stay true, and how the documents in this Knowledge Center are built, dated, shared, and credited.

Documentation lets someone use, run, or change a project without asking its author. It's written once, in one place, kept next to the code it describes, and updated in the same change as the code.

Every project has

FileForContains
README.mdAnyone arriving at the projectWhat it is, who it's for, its status, how to run, test, and deploy it, and its license
CHANGELOG.mdPeople using itWhat changed in each release, newest first. See versioning
LICENSEAnyone reusing itThe license text, plus NOTICE when required
SECURITY.mdAnyone who finds a problemHow to report it privately. See the security disclosure policy

Larger projects add:

FileForContains
VCS-ETIQUETTE.md or CONTRIBUTING.mdContributorsAny rules stricter than the version control standard
Decision recordsFuture maintainersWhy a significant choice was made, the options considered, and what would change it
RunbooksWhoever operates itStep-by-step tasks such as deploy, roll back, restore, and rotate a secret

Write by purpose

Following Diátaxis, each document does one of four jobs, and doesn't mix them:

  • Tutorial: learning by doing, for a newcomer.
  • How-to: steps to finish a specific task.
  • Reference: exact facts to look up, such as commands, settings, and fields.
  • Explanation: why things are the way they are.

A README usually holds a short version of each and links out when one grows.

Decision records

Write one when a choice is costly to reverse: a database, a framework, a hosting model, a license. Keep it to a page: the context, the decision, the options rejected and why, and what would make us revisit it. Number them and never delete one. A changed decision gets a new record that replaces the old one. The tool and architecture decision form is a template.

Runbooks

Prerequisites come first, then commands in the order they're run, each with what you should see and what to do if you don't. Commands are copied exactly and tested. A runbook nobody has followed is a draft.

Keeping docs true

  • Docs change in the same commit as the behavior they describe.
  • A checked fact beats a remembered one. Commands in a README should be run before a release.
  • One source for each fact. Link to it instead of copying it, so it can't drift. That's why neon1's public words live once, in neon1-corpus.

Documents in this Knowledge Center

Everything here is written once in neon1-corpus, as Markdown, and read from there by the website, the Knowledge Center and its PDFs, and Neo. Each document is built the same way, so a reader always knows where to look.

What every document carries

PartWhat it saysWhere readers see it
TitleWhat the document is, in plain wordsThe page heading and the PDF's title
SummaryOne sentence on what it covers and who it helpsUnder the title, on its card, and in search results
TypeWhich kind of document it is (below)The facts under the title
EditionX.Y, raised as described in versioningThe facts, and the PDF's footer
PublishedWhen the content first appeared, from its real historyThe facts
UpdatedWhen it last changed in substance, shown once it differs from PublishedThe facts, and the date at the top of the PDF
ForWho it's written for, when that isn't everyoneThe facts

Dates are never moved to look newer or older than they are. A typo fix doesn't change Updated or the edition.

Kinds of document

TypeIts jobShape
PageSay what neon1 is or offersShort sections, in the order a newcomer asks
StandardSay how neon1 works and whyWhat I do, then the reason, then Sources
GuideHelp someone finish a taskWho it's for, steps, what to do when it goes wrong, Sources
Case studyShow real work honestlyNeeds, Execute, Observe, Normalize, with limits stated
FAQAnswer the questions people askOne question per heading, the answer in its first sentence
PolicySay what's done with information, and rightsShort version first, then sections by question
Template and formBe filled inLabeled blanks and checkboxes, no advice mixed in
ExampleShow a template or form filled inMarked fictional, linked to its blank
ComparisonPoint to other good optionsWho each fits, and when another provider is better

Sharing and reuse

  • Link to the page. Every document has a fixed address under neon1.tech/knowledge/, and each section has its own anchor, so a link can point at the exact part.
  • Hand over the PDF. Documents marked for it print to a PDF with the same text, dated, with its edition in the footer and a link back to the live version, since a PDF travels on its own.
  • Copy word for word. Documents are shared under CC BY-ND 4.0, credited "© neon1 LLC (neon1.tech)". Blank templates and forms may also be filled in and adapted for your own work.

Credit where it's due

The practice described here builds on standards bodies, government guides, and practitioners who published what they learned. Documents name them where they're used and list them under Sources, following the writing standard. Where I learn from gathers them in one place.

Sources

  • Diátaxis, by Daniele Procida: four kinds of documentation, each with its own job.
  • Write the Docs guide, from the Write the Docs community: docs as code, and keeping documentation next to what it describes.
  • Documenting architecture decisions, by Michael Nygard: the short decision record this standard uses.
  • Keep a Changelog 1.1.0: changelogs written for people, newest first.
  • Google SRE workbook, from Google: runbooks and on-call practice for services that must keep running.
